Simulation models for teaching economics, with interactive pages to explore
them. The code behind each model is in the
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/jomichell/teaching-models).

The models were written for the final-year module Economic Theory and Policy
(ETP), and follow its first topic: technology, automation, work and distribution.
If you are an ETP student, start with the [guide for ETP students](etp.qmd),
which links each model to the lectures and workshops that use it.

## Production and distribution

Who gets what, and why? The first three pages build up the marginal-productivity
view, in which technology and the prices of inputs decide the shares of labour and
capital. The last gives the alternative, in which firms' pricing power decides
them.

- Cobb-Douglas production function, in two steps:
  1. [isoquants](cobb-douglas/index.qmd)
  2. [cost minimisation and factor shares](cobb-douglas/cost.qmd)
- [CES production, the elasticity of substitution and factor shares](ces/shares.qmd):
  does cheaper capital lower the labour share?
- [Markups and the wage share](markup/index.qmd)

## Growth

Where does growth in output per worker come from? In the Solow model, saving and
investment raise the *level* of output per worker, but long-run growth comes only
from technology, which the model leaves unexplained.

- Solow growth model, in four steps:
  1. [constant technology](solow/index.qmd)
  2. [constant technology, with an investment rate shock](solow/shock.qmd)
  3. [growing technology and effective labour](solow/effective.qmd)
  4. [growing technology, with an investment rate shock](solow/effective-shock.qmd)

## Technology and AI

How much could AI add to output? If tasks are complements, output is held back by
the tasks that cannot be automated.

- [CES production and weak links](ces/index.qmd), following Jones (2026),
  *AI and Our Economic Future*
